description: Test your knowledge of MI1.{1-2,10,12-13} | General Microbiology I: History, Morphology, Sterilisation & Staining.

cards.text: State Koch's four postulates that establish a causal relationship between a microorganism and disease.
cards.answer: 1. Organism found in all cases of disease. 2. Isolated in pure culture from host. 3. Pure culture reproduces disease in healthy host. 4. Organism re-isolated from experimentally infected host.

cards.text: Who disproved spontaneous generation, developed germ theory, and pioneered vaccination with the swan-neck flask experiment?
cards.answer: Louis Pasteur (1860s). His work proved that microbes cause specific diseases and established the scientific basis for vaccines (cholera, anthrax, rabies) and pasteurisation.

tip.tip: Pasteur's swan-neck flask = air carries microbes, not spontaneous generation

cards.answer: Pathogenicity = capacity of a microbe to cause disease (qualitative, yes/no). Virulence = degree of severity of disease caused (quantitative, measured by mortality/morbidity rates).

cards.text: Name four major virulence determinants and give one example for each.
cards.answer: Adhesins (e.g. fimbriae of E. coli), Invasins (e.g. M protein of Streptococcus), Toxins (e.g. exotoxins/endotoxins), Capsules (e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae resists phagocytosis).

cards.text: Define the four ecological roles of microorganisms in humans and provide one clinical example.
cards.answer: Commensal (neutral/beneficial; viridans streptococci), Mutualist (mutual benefit; E. coli makes Vitamin K), Opportunist (pathogenic only if defences fail; Candida in immunocompromised), Pathogen (always disease-causing; Mycobacterium tuberculosis).

cards.text: Which scientist demonstrated that malaria is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes and when?
cards.answer: Sir Ronald Ross, working in India in 1897. This discovery earned him the Nobel Prize in 1902 and was a landmark in understanding vector-borne disease transmission.

tip.tip: Ross → Malaria vector; worked in India; 1897

cards.text: What was Alexander Fleming's observation in 1928 that led to the antibiotic era?
cards.answer: Fleming observed that Penicillium mould lysed Staphylococcus colonies on an agar plate, leading to the discovery and isolation of penicillin — the first widely used antibiotic.

tip.tip: Fleming's mouldy plate = contamination becomes breakthrough

cards.text: List three physiological functions of the human microbiome that maintain health.
cards.answer: Competitive exclusion of pathogens, maturation of innate and adaptive immunity, synthesis of short-chain fatty acids and vitamins (especially Vitamin K by E. coli).
